Japan wants to wrap the Moon in a belt of solar panels 6,800 miles long and beam unlimited clean energy back to Earth forever. And the idea is less science fiction than it sounds.

The concept is called the Luna Ring, proposed by Japanese construction firm Shimizu Corporation. The ring would stretch along the entire lunar equator, ranging in width from a few kilometers to 400 kilometers at its widest point. The Moon has no atmosphere, no clouds, no weather, and no night cycle at its equator. One side or the other is always in direct sunlight. That means uninterrupted solar power generation around the clock, every single day, forever.

Solar cells on the lunar equator would convert sunlight into electricity, cables would carry that power to the Earth-facing side of the Moon, and from there microwave beams and high energy lasers would transmit it down to receiving stations on the ground.

The numbers are staggering. In its most expansive form the project could generate up to 13,000 terawatts of energy per hour, a level that would far exceed current global electricity needs if realized at scale. For context, total global energy consumption today is around 18 terawatts. The Luna Ring would produce roughly 700 times that.

Construction would be handled by robots controlled from Earth, using materials already on the Moon. Lunar soil would be turned into concrete, glass fiber, and structural blocks built entirely on site. No massive cargo missions required.

The obvious questions are cost, feasibility, and timeline. Shimizu has not secured funding, received no official endorsement from space agencies, and has no active development timeline. The technology to beam gigawatts of power accurately across 238,000 miles of space does not yet exist at scale.

But neither did GPS once. Neither did the internet. Neither did landing on the Moon.

The energy crisis is real. The climate crisis is real. And sometimes the most important ideas are the ones that sound completely impossible until they suddenly are not.
